fixes.explanation: Yes, frightened. The king says, “I had a dream, and it frightened me; while I was in my bed, the images and visions in my mind alarmed me.” He was lying in bed, and the dream still got to him. Nobody walks away from a dream like that saying, "Well, that was nice."

That's what he says. The king tells Daniel, “…I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in you and that no mystery baffles you.” Those are the king's own words about Daniel. He brings the dream to Daniel after the other wise men could not interpret it (Daniel 4:7).

Danger isn't in the dream's picture of the tree. The king says the beasts of the field “found shelter” under it. Later the watcher orders, “Let the beasts flee from under it…” (Daniel 4:14). Under the full tree, it was a safe place to be.

Starved is the opposite of what the king describes. He says “…its fruit was abundant, and upon it was food for all.” and that “…from it every creature was fed.” Nobody is going hungry around this tree. I'd say that's a tree with a very good reputation.

False, and good catch. The watcher says, “But leave the stump with its roots in the ground, with a band of iron and bronze around it, in the tender grass of the field.” The stump and its roots stay in the ground. It's a tree that's been cut down and still isn't finished.

Nobody gets sent home. When Daniel is perplexed, the king says, “Belteshazzar, do not let the dream or its interpretation alarm you.” Daniel answers right there. Nothing in the text says the king tells him to come back later.

Advisers aren't mentioned in Daniel's answer. He says, “may the dream apply to those who hate you, and its interpretation to your enemies!” He wishes it on those who hate the king and on his enemies. The wise men had already failed to interpret the dream (Daniel 4:7), but Daniel doesn't aim anything at them.

Straight to his face. Daniel says, “…you, O king, are that tree! For you have become great and strong; your greatness has grown to reach the sky, and your dominion extends to the ends of the earth.” The tree that grew large and strong, with its top in the sky, is the king. Daniel doesn't dance around it.

It's actually true. Daniel says, “…this is the decree that the Most High has issued against my lord the king…” Think about standing in front of the king of Babylon with that message. I'd have been looking for the nearest exit, and I'd have had to hop there on my base.

Youth isn't on the list, friend. Daniel says, “…your kingdom will be restored to you as soon as you acknowledge that Heaven rules.” That's what the stump and its roots stand for. The stump left in the ground is the hope inside the hard news.

The king doesn't say that. He says, “Is this not Babylon the Great, which I myself have built as a royal residence by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” He talks about what he built and credits himself, and nothing about the city being too big for one king. It's a long way from where he started his letter.

It's actually true. The voice from heaven says, “It is decreed to you, King Nebuchadnezzar, that the kingdom has departed from you.” It comes while the words are still in the king's mouth. His boast about Babylon hadn't even finished echoing off the roof.

The watcher isn't in this part. The king says, “…I, Nebuchadnezzar, looked up to heaven, and my sanity was restored to me.” The watcher appeared in the dream and called out his orders (Daniel 4:13-14). Here it's the king who looks up.
